A team of High school students trying to add their mark in the world of hackathons. Combining strong foundations in STEM subjects with Python capabilities, our team exclusively is built to embed physical mechanics and software logic.
About to engineer something impactful for the astronauts!
summary: Halfway to Mars, a message to Earth can take 20 minutes, and crew members are not medical specialists. OrbitFit is an offline crew health station built to run on standard flight laptops or tablets—requiring zero internet connection, external wearables, or ground support.Using a single low-overhead camera, OrbitFit tracks workout mechanics in real time, scoring squat depth, tempo, and body symmetry. Its interactive Gravity Sliders let astronauts dial in exact planetary forces—from Deep Space microgravity (0g) to Earth (1.0g), the Moon (0.166g), Mars (0.38g), or custom environments—instantly recalculating machine resistance, bottom-hold tempos, and weekly volume to prevent bone and muscle loss.Crew members perform 30-second daily check-ins, log vitals, and monitor radiation exposure against NASA-STD-3001 career limits. Plain-language alerts explain health risks using NASA Human Research Program evidence, paired with microgravity-adapted emergency CPR guides. A digital twin model predicts fatigue and bone density trends, buffering compact telemetry packets locally until a comms window opens. Beyond spaceflight, OrbitFit provides an offline healthcare blueprint for isolated Earth communities.
details:
What it does

  • Astronaut view: a status at a glance, a daily routine with a streak (check-in, vital signs, camera workout) and live workout feedback with a rep counter and one plain cue ("Go deeper", "Lower more slowly").
  • Gravity engine: the exercise plan scales with gravity (Earth, ISS, transit, Moon, Mars, or a custom gravity slider). Lower gravity means the exercise device adds back the load gravity no longer gives (W = m·g).
  • Vital signs and radiation: step-by-step guides for heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, blood sugar and oxygen saturation; the daily dosimeter dose and mission total against NASA's 600 mSv career limit.
  • Emergency: yes/no triage gives a priority (Emergency / Urgent / Monitor) and tickable guides. In microgravity the CPR guide starts with securing the patient and bracing yourself.
  • Health guides: a clickable body map: what each body area does, what spaceflight does to it, and how to measure it.
  • Forecast: a digital twin (Monte Carlo of a sleep model coupled with a motion-sickness model) forecasts fatigue; a bone-loss projection shows the effect of exercise; daily energy needs are estimated.
  • Crew Medical Officer: crew overview, trends against each person's baseline, alert log, notes, and CSV export/import of the offline logbook.
  • Report to Earth: a 6 KB packet waits for a comms window; a simulated link adds delay, blackouts and retry.

How it works

MediaPipe pose estimation runs on the device and turns body points into knee angles. A rep detector counts reps and measures tempo and asymmetry. To save battery the pose model runs on about 1 frame in 7 (about 75% fewer model calls, same rep count). Each person's baseline is the median of their first valid sessions, and rules compare recent values with it; several warning signs together escalate to "Needs action". Every rep is saved to a local SQLite logbook the moment it ends, so a crash loses nothing.

Benefits and impact

Works with no internet, no wearables and no ground contact. Plain language for non-doctors, never claims a diagnosis, and every simulated part is labelled. Beyond space, it could support remote communities with little access to health services.

Tools

Python, Streamlit, MediaPipe, OpenCV, SQLite, pandas, Plotly, NumPy, pytest (328 automated tests).

Creativity and factors considered

Gravity-aware exercise plans, a camera instead of wearables, offline-first design for comms blackouts, alerts that compare each astronaut with themself rather than a population average, and microgravity-specific emergency steps.
